lesson.title: Speaking Statistics to a Non-Statistician
lesson.summary: Consolidates the precise interpretation language for confidence intervals, general hypothesis tests, chi-square conclusions, and regression slope conclusions into one toolkit for explaining results accurately to any audience.
lesson.body:
Across this course you learned to interpret four different kinds of statistical output: a confidence interval, a general hypothesis test conclusion, a chi-square conclusion for independence, homogeneity, or goodness of fit, and a regression slope conclusion. Each has its own precise phrasing, and mixing them up is one of the most common ways a technically correct calculation turns into a misleading statement once it reaches another person.

It is worth reviewing each one alongside its most common misstatement. A confidence interval is about capturing the parameter across repeated sampling, the correct phrasing is that the method produces intervals that capture the true parameter a certain percent of the time in the long run, not that a particular already-computed interval has a 95 percent probability of containing the parameter, since once the interval exists, the parameter either is or is not inside it. A general hypothesis test's p-value is the probability of getting a statistic this extreme or more extreme if the null hypothesis is true, never the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true. A chi-square conclusion should be phrased in terms of association between two categorical variables, or a difference in distribution shape across groups, never in terms of one variable causing the other. A regression slope conclusion of convincing evidence of a linear relationship means there is evidence the true slope differs from zero, not proof that x causes y, and any prediction made outside the range of observed x-values should be flagged as extrapolation, which carries extra risk of being wrong.

Suppose a chi-square test for independence is used to examine whether preferred class format, online versus in-person, is associated with whether a student completes an AP Statistics course. A jargon-heavy version might say, chi-square equals 8.7 with 1 degree of freedom, p equals 0.003, so we reject the null hypothesis of independence. A clear version for a school principal instead says, students who took the course online completed it at a noticeably different rate than students who took it in person, and this gap is large enough that it is very unlikely to be due to chance alone. Both versions describe the same test, but only the second one is actually communicating something.

Match the level of detail to the audience. For a technical audience, include the test statistic, degrees of freedom, and exact p-value so the analysis can be checked. For a general audience, lead with the plain-language conclusion and a confidence interval to convey the size of the effect, and push the formula-level detail into an appendix or footnote rather than the opening sentence. Whichever audience you are writing for, never drop the uncertainty language, convincing evidence, confident, approximately, since replacing hedged language with flat certainty is the single most common way an otherwise correct analysis turns into an overclaim once someone repeats it secondhand.

With these translation habits in hand for each individual procedure, the next section assembles the full pipeline that produced them in the first place, stating the question, planning and justifying a procedure, doing the calculation, and concluding with exactly this kind of precise language, into the single four-step process used on every AP Statistics inference question.
